title: Berkshire 2001: Float economics, the three underwriting rules, and owning mistakes at General Re and Dexter
summary: Buffett's 2001 letter covers a bad year: 9/11 losses and General Re's underreserving. It explains how to value an insurer by float, its cost and underwriting discipline, and gives candid mea culpas. It also covers owner-aligned management, buying from trusted managers, and his contempt for EBITDA and options.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by the amount of float, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Float is only valuable if its cost is below what you would pay to get funds elsewhere.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Insurance winners stick to underwriting discipline: stay in your circle of competence, cap aggregation, avoid moral risk.
principles.quote: What counts in this business is underwriting discipline. The winners are those that unfailingly stick to three key principles

principles.text: Predicting a danger is worthless unless you act on it; take action, not just forecasts.
principles.quote: I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn’t count; building arks does.

principles.text: Outstanding long-term results come mainly from avoiding dumb decisions, not from brilliant ones.
principles.quote: Just as is the case in investing, insurers produce outstanding long-term results primarily by avoiding dumb decisions, rather than by making brilliant ones.

principles.text: Align managers as true owners who bear downside and a cost of capital, not option holders who can reprice.
principles.quote: As they would not be if they had options, all of these managers are true owners. They face the downside of decisions as well as the upside. They incur a cost of capital.
